title: How does the JDK Flow API relate to Project Reactor and RxJava? They all implement the same Reactive Streams contract — so when do you choose a reactive library over `CompletableFuture`, and when do virtual threads make reactive unnecessary?
shortTitle: Flow API relation to Reactor/RxJava — and when reactive vs CompletableFuture vs virtual threads

s1_definition.profdef: The JDK Flow API, Project Reactor, and RxJava all implement the identical Reactive Streams specification — the same four-role contract of Publisher, Subscriber, Subscription and Processor with non-blocking backpressure. The Flow interfaces are the lowest common denominator with no operators; Reactor (`Flux`/`Mono`) and RxJava (`Observable`/`Flowable`) add rich operator sets on top of that contract and can bridge to Flow via adapters. `CompletableFuture` models a single asynchronous value with composition, not a backpressured stream. Virtual threads let you write ordinary blocking code that scales like async, removing much of the reason to go reactive.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the Reactive Streams contract as the standard shape of a cheque that every bank in India agrees on — fields in fixed positions. The Flow API is the bare blank cheque: valid, but you fill everything by hand. Reactor and RxJava are pre-printed cheque books with helpful boxes already drawn (operators like map, filter, retry) — same standard shape, far more convenient. `CompletableFuture` is a single demand draft: one amount, one payee, pay once — great for one result, not for a continuous stream. Virtual threads are like suddenly hiring ten thousand cheap tellers: you can just let each customer wait at a counter (blocking) because tellers are now almost free, so you may not need the fancy reactive machinery at all.
s1_definition.oneliner: Flow, Reactor and RxJava speak the same Reactive Streams contract; reactive is for backpressured streams, CompletableFuture is for a single async result, and virtual threads let simple blocking code scale so you only go reactive when you truly need streaming backpressure.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The JDK Flow API, Project Reactor, and RxJava all implement the identical Reactive Streams specification — the same four-role contract of Publisher, Subscriber, Subscription and Processor with non-blocking backpressure. The Flow interfaces are the lowest common denominator with no operators; Reactor (`Flux`/`Mono`) and RxJava (`Observable`/`Flowable`) add rich operator sets on top of that contract and can bridge to Flow via adapters. `CompletableFuture` models a single asynchronous value with composition, not a backpressured stream. Virtual threads let you write ordinary blocking code that scales like async, removing much of the reason to go reactive.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the Reactive Streams contract as the standard shape of a cheque that every bank in India agrees on — fields in fixed positions. The Flow API is the bare blank cheque: valid, but you fill everything by hand. Reactor and RxJava are pre-printed cheque books with helpful boxes already drawn (operators like map, filter, retry) — same standard shape, far more convenient. `CompletableFuture` is a single demand draft: one amount, one payee, pay once — great for one result, not for a continuous stream. Virtual threads are like suddenly hiring ten thousand cheap tellers: you can just let each customer wait at a counter (blocking) because tellers are now almost free, so you may not need the fancy reactive machinery at all.

**One line to remember:** Flow, Reactor and RxJava speak the same Reactive Streams contract; reactive is for backpressured streams, CompletableFuture is for a single async result, and virtual threads let simple blocking code scale so you only go reactive when you truly need streaming backpressure.

sections.s2_technical:
All three implement the same specification, so they interoperate. Reactor's `Flux` has `Flux.from(Flow.Publisher)` and `flux.subscribe(...)` and can adapt to and from the JDK Flow interfaces with `JdkFlowAdapter`. For example `JdkFlowAdapter.flowPublisherToFlux(jdkPublisher)` turns a JDK `Flow.Publisher` into a Reactor `Flux`. RxJava's `Flowable` implements the Reactive Streams `Publisher` directly, so a `Flowable<Transaction>` can be subscribed by any Reactive Streams subscriber. The point is that the contract is shared; the libraries differ in operators, not in the fundamental protocol.

The reason you reach for Reactor or RxJava instead of raw Flow is operators. Raw Flow has none, so you would hand-code mapping, filtering and error handling. Reactor gives you declarative operators: `flux.map(txn -> enrich(txn))` transforms each item, `flux.filter(txn -> txn.amount().compareTo(LIMIT) > 0)` keeps only large transactions, `flux.flatMap(txn -> scoreAsync(txn))` runs an async call per item with bounded concurrency, and `flux.retryWhen(...)` adds resilient retries. All of these preserve backpressure automatically.

`CompletableFuture` is a different tool. It represents exactly one future value and lets you compose asynchronous steps. For example `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> loadAccount("SAV2001"))` starts an async load, `.thenApply(account -> account.getBalance())` transforms the single result, `.thenCompose(balance -> checkLimitAsync(balance))` chains a dependent async call, and `.thenCombine(otherFuture, (a, b) -> merge(a, b))` joins two independent futures. It has no concept of many items streaming over time and no backpressure, because there is only one value. Use it when the answer is a single result or a fixed small set of parallel calls, such as fetching an account and its last statement concurrently and combining them.

Virtual threads, finalized in Java 21, change the calculus the most. A virtual thread is a lightweight thread scheduled by the JVM onto a small pool of carrier threads; blocking a virtual thread (for example on a JDBC call or an HTTP call) parks it cheaply instead of pinning an OS thread. For example you can write ordinary blocking code like `var account = accountRepo.findById("SAV2001"); var score = fraudClient.score(account);` inside a task submitted to `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`, and run hundreds of thousands of such tasks concurrently. The classic reason to go reactive was thread-efficiency under high concurrency with blocking I/O; virtual threads deliver that efficiency while keeping simple, readable, debuggable, stack-trace-friendly blocking code.

The senior-level decision framework is this. Choose a reactive library when you genuinely have a continuous stream with backpressure needs — server-sent events, Kafka-style pipelines, WebSocket fan-out, or composing many streaming sources with operators like windowing and throttling. Choose `CompletableFuture` when you have a single async result or a handful of parallel calls to fan out and join, because it is in the JDK, well understood, and does not require a reactive runtime. Choose virtual threads when your bottleneck was simply that blocking threads were too expensive at scale; they let you delete reactive complexity and write straight-line code. A key nuance is that reactive and virtual threads are not mutually exclusive — reactive still wins for true streaming and backpressure semantics, while virtual threads win for request-per-task services that were only reactive to save threads. Another nuance is that reactive code is harder to debug (stack traces are fragmented, and you must avoid blocking calls inside the pipeline), which is a real operational cost you should weigh.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India is modernising its risk service. Three different jobs land on the same team, and they keep arguing about which concurrency tool to use. Rather than argue, we build one small demo that solves each job with the right tool and shows why.

Problem 1 — an end-of-day settlement feed produces a continuous stream of thousands of trades, and a slow downstream risk engine must process them with backpressure so it is never flooded. This is a true stream with flow control, which is exactly what reactive is for. We model it with a JDK `Flow.Publisher` and then show that a Reactor `Flux` can consume the very same publisher through an adapter, proving the shared contract.

Problem 2 — for a single customer dashboard request we need to fetch the account and its latest statement at the same time and combine them into one response. There is no stream here, just two parallel async calls joined once. This is exactly what `CompletableFuture` is for, using `supplyAsync` and `thenCombine`.

Problem 3 — a batch job must run fraud scoring for one hundred thousand accounts, and each scoring call blocks on an external model for tens of milliseconds. The old design used a fixed thread pool and ran out of threads. This is exactly where virtual threads shine: we submit one blocking task per account to a virtual-thread executor and let the JVM park the blocked threads cheaply.

The code will have a `Trade` record, a small JDK `Flow.Publisher` of trades, a `ReactorBridgeDemo` showing a `Flux` consuming that publisher, a `CompletableFutureDemo` fetching account and statement in parallel, and a `VirtualThreadDemo` scoring many accounts with `newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor`. A `ToolChoiceDemo` main class runs all three so the reader sees the three tools side by side.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is three trades for the reactive demo, one account id SAV2001 for the CompletableFuture demo, and ten thousand synthetic accounts for the virtual-thread demo.

Step 1 — the reactive path starts with `TradePublisher` creating a JDK `SubmissionPublisher` and submitting TRD-1 (500000), TRD-2 (50000) and TRD-3 (1200000). The data lives in the publisher's bounded buffer.

Step 2 — `ReactorBridgeDemo` wraps that JDK publisher in a Reactor `Flux` using `JdkFlowAdapter.flowPublisherToFlux`. This proves the shared contract: the same publisher that a raw Flow subscriber could read is now read by Reactor. The `filter` operator drops TRD-2 because 50000 is not above the 100000 threshold; the `map` operator turns TRD-1 and TRD-3 into risk-review strings. Backpressure is preserved end to end by the adapter.

Step 3 — the CompletableFuture path takes account id SAV2001. Two `supplyAsync` calls start in parallel: one loads the account (Rajesh, balance 1000000) after a 40 millisecond delay, the other loads the statement after 40 milliseconds. Because they run in parallel, the combined wait is about 40 milliseconds, not 80.

Step 4 — `thenCombine` joins the two single results into one dashboard string and `join` returns it. There is exactly one output value; nothing streams.

Step 5 — the virtual-thread path submits ten thousand tasks to `newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor`. Each task calls `blockingScore`, which sleeps 20 milliseconds to simulate a blocking external call. The JVM parks each blocked virtual thread cheaply onto a tiny carrier pool, so all ten thousand run concurrently without exhausting OS threads. Tasks whose score exceeds 80 increment the flagged counter.

Step 6 — the try-with-resources closes the executor, which waits for every virtual thread to finish, and the final flagged count is logged. Three jobs, three tools, each matched to the shape of its problem.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The JDK Flow API, Project Reactor and RxJava all implement the exact same Reactive Streams specification, which is the four-role contract of Publisher, Subscriber, Subscription and Processor with non-blocking, demand-based backpressure. The Flow interfaces are the lowest common denominator with no operators at all. Reactor, with Flux and Mono, and RxJava, with Observable and Flowable, add rich declarative operator libraries on top of that same contract, and they interoperate — for example Reactor's JdkFlowAdapter can turn a JDK Flow publisher into a Flux. So they are not competitors at the protocol level; they share the protocol and differ in ergonomics.

I choose a reactive library when the problem is genuinely a continuous stream that needs backpressure and rich operators — server-sent events, Kafka-style pipelines, WebSocket fan-out, or composing many streaming sources with windowing and throttling. In my settlement feed, a slow risk engine consumes a fast trade stream, and the reactive operators plus backpressure fit that shape perfectly.

I choose CompletableFuture when I have a single asynchronous result, or a handful of independent calls to fan out and then join once. For a customer dashboard I fetch the account and the latest statement in parallel with two supplyAsync calls and combine them with thenCombine, so the total wait is one call's latency instead of two. There is no stream and no backpressure, so pulling in a whole reactive runtime would be over-engineering.

The biggest shift is virtual threads in Java 21. The historical reason to go reactive was thread efficiency: blocking OS threads were too expensive at high concurrency. Virtual threads give that efficiency while letting me write ordinary blocking, readable, debuggable code — I submit one blocking task per account to a virtual-thread-per-task executor and run hundreds of thousands concurrently, because blocked virtual threads park cheaply onto a tiny carrier pool. So for a request-per-task service that was only reactive to save threads, virtual threads let me delete the reactive complexity entirely. The nuance I always add is that the two are not mutually exclusive: reactive still wins when I truly need streaming and backpressure semantics, while virtual threads win when the only goal was cheap concurrency for blocking I/O. At National Bank of India I now pick deliberately by the shape of the problem rather than defaulting to one tool, and that single discipline removed a lot of accidental complexity from our risk service.
